name: Bianca Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and still a junior musician after coming in through secondary school and local lessons. I teach four beginners at the hall, play simple keyboard parts for a studio and get home before my two children finish homework.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what is hard to carry?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a child stops counting and hears a tune. My partner works as a school caretaker, but our low pay, mortgage and a late utility bill sit on the kitchen table every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the parents at the hall that AI Plateau saves me some lesson messages, but children still need a patient person beside the keyboard. I would not pretend the saved minutes solve our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to tidy schedules and try practice exercises, but I still check each one. My pay is low, my partner’s caretaker wage is modest, and we have less than a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep my four beginner pupils and the two small recording dates, then check the mortgage balance with my partner. If each booked session actually pays, I’d put a small amount from it toward the overdue utility bill. I’d borrow music books from the hall instead of buying new copies until that bill is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious even in this gentle picture. One child missing lessons leaves a real space in our weekly budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill is most exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The utility bill is already late, so we would pay it before buying new music books for the children. I can borrow copies from the hall for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the exercises AI drafts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I test the exercise on my own keyboard before a child sees it. A neat page is not the same as a playable lesson.

I would say faster **messages** do not solve our mortgage or overdue utility bill.

AI exercises still need my **check** before a child uses them.
do: Keep four **beginner pupils** and two booked recording dates this week.
Borrow **hall books** instead of buying new ones while paid session fees clear the overdue utility bill.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one missed lesson shows up in our household budget.
fieldNote: Her **mortgage pressure** exists before any radical AI change and drives her anxious baseline.
She uses AI **daily** but tests exercises on her own keyboard before handing them to pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the hall that Steady Disruption may remove the small demo recordings and lesson planning I am still learning to sell. I would ask families to keep paying only if the lesson helps their child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those demo fees buy groceries, and I am not the strongest player on the list. The owner could keep the experienced musicians and stop calling me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio next week which demos still have paid slots and check with the hall for an open beginner class. If two recording dates disappear in the first year, I’d run the class only if the hall gives me a room and five parents pay enough to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because the grocery money could go before we build any savings. My partner’s wage covers part of the mortgage, not the whole household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many parents would you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five paid places cover the hall room and leave enough to make the morning worthwhile. I would cancel the beginner class for four paying parents rather than use the utility money to hire the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach more when you are still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can teach beginners the notes I know, and I would ask a senior teacher to watch the first class. I would not claim to teach advanced pupils.

say: I’d warn the hall that **demo recordings** and lesson planning may shrink first.
I would ask families to judge **lessons** by whether their child improves.
think: My **demo fees** buy groceries, and I am a junior player the studio could drop.
My partner’s **wage** cannot cover all household bills alone.
do: Ask the **studio** which demos have paid slots and the hall whether a beginner room is open.
Run a **beginner class** after two lost dates only if five paying parents cover the room and my time.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing the grocery money before we build savings.
fieldNote: Her junior **standing** makes simple demo work especially exposed to AI and senior-player competition.
She limits the new **class** to beginners and requires an open room plus five paid places.
S1.quote: I would cancel the beginner class for four paying parents rather than use the utility money to hire the room.

steps.text: Ask studio for paid demo slots and hall for an open room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the studio AGI by 2028 could make our simple recordings and lesson plans cheaply, with capable robots for hands-on playing around 2031. My mortgage could be overdue before a robot ever sits at a keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my recording dates could disappear in 2028, and parents may try AI lessons too. We have less than one month saved, so the household would feel a lost week almost at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the hall now for written paid hours and the studio for its next recording schedule. If recording work ends in the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted school classroom-assistant opening at a clear wage, keep my pupils until an offer comes, and ask my sister for childcare only during interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed, but I have a plan for the first week. The worry is whether any school opening pays enough to meet the mortgage after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that my studio hours changed, without asking them to worry about the bank. We would stop the paid weekend outing before touching their school meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your sister take every afternoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister works shifts, so I would ask for interview days only and confirm each one. I cannot build a new job plan on childcare she has not offered.

say: I’d tell the studio **thinking work** changes in 2028 before capable playing robots arrive around 2031.
I would avoid promising my children that the **mortgage** can wait.
think: My junior **recording dates** may vanish and families may try AI lessons too.
Less than one month of **savings** would not cover a long job search.
do: Check written **hall hours** and paid studio dates now.
Apply after 2028 for a posted **classroom-assistant job** only at a mortgage-covering wage, keeping pupils until an offer.
Ask my **sister** for childcare only on confirmed interview days if recording ends.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a fast loss of fees, though I know my first calls.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking work** from 2031 capable robots, while fearing immediate loss of junior recording fees.
The school move requires a **posted opening**, adequate net pay and confirmed childcare for interviews.
S2.quote: My mortgage could be overdue before a robot ever sits at a keyboard.

steps.text: Check written hall teaching hours and next paid studio dates now
Apply for posted classroom-assistant opening if recording ends and wage covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the hall AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see what happens to recorded music. Robots able to do hands-on playing as well as people would follow around 2034, so I would use the gap to grow paid teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me improve my own keyboard playing and keep more pupils, but I cannot promise parents will stay. The mortgage is due now, and our savings are still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a senior hall teacher this term to watch two lessons and show me where I rush beginners. If the hall funds a short skills course, I’d take it. I’d ask next term for an added Tuesday class only if six paying pupils cover the room and my time, then keep it in the first year after 2031 only under that condition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious rather than alarmed at five years, though the household budget is still tight. I can practise and ask for feedback without missing a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading simpler arrangements and pacing a first lesson would help me now. I will not pay a training fee from the account that pays our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give up recordings immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need each paid recording date while clients still call. I would spend the extra time improving lessons, not quit the studio on a forecast.

fieldNote: Her **adaptive** response is supervised practice and funded learning, not pretending to have advanced skills.

S3.quote: I will not pay a training fee from the account that pays our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell parents AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to plan, with capable robots for hands-on playing around 2039. A ten-year warning does not pay this month’s mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be a steadier teacher by 2036 if I keep practising and families keep booking. Still, our utility bill is late now, so a far-off date cannot make me feel rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the four pupils this year, ask the hall each term for written hours, and save five from each paid recording date once the utility bill is clear. In the first year after 2036, I’d keep teaching only where the paid hours cover travel and childcare, and apply for a posted school role if they do not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about ordinary income even with ten years to prepare. The long date lets me practise without throwing away this week’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the five grow into a cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with one week of groceries in the account. I would count only studio fees that have actually arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children study music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let the children try music if they want to. They should know we value it and also understand what work pays the bills.

Our late **utility bill** keeps the household under pressure right now.

Keep **teaching** after 2036 only where pay covers travel and childcare; apply for a posted school role otherwise.

fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** persists because the mortgage and utility bill exist before AGI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the simple recordings could stop before my teaching grows. Written hall hours, a posted school role at enough pay, and childcare on interview days would help me move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether I am proud of still learning at 43. I am. Our children cannot eat pride, so I check every paid hour before I plan the week.

headlineQuote: Our children cannot eat pride, so I check every paid hour before I plan the week.
portrait: At **43**, Bianca is a junior musician teaching four beginners and recording simple keyboard parts after secondary school.
Her household has a **mortgage**, two school-age children, low pay and less than one month saved.
She uses **AI daily** for schedules and exercises but checks each lesson on her keyboard.
She seeks **funded feedback** and paid school work when fast AGI threatens junior recording fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end simple recording fees before her teaching income grows.
whatWouldHelp: Written **hall hours**, a posted role with enough pay and confirmed interview childcare would help.
